description_ru: Забавная история о поездке, в которой навигатор и водитель никак не могут договориться.
text:
My satnav and I have not spoken to each other for three days, except to exchange the minimum of necessary insults. It began, as these things so often do, with a misunderstanding about a roundabout.

We were driving to a wedding in a village I will not name, partly to protect its dignity and partly because I cannot pronounce it. The satnav, who speaks in the calm voice of a woman who has never been late for anything, instructed me to "take the third exit". I counted the exits. There appeared to be five, one of which was a car park, one a field and one a sort of suggestion. I chose the one that looked most like a road. "Recalculating," she said, in a tone that managed to be both patient and devastating.

For the next twenty minutes we were engaged in a polite war. She suggested U-turns; I ignored them. She offered an alternative route; I declined it on principle. At one point she told me to "continue straight for four miles", and I did so, trusting her, until the road narrowed into a lane, the lane narrowed into a track, and the track ended at a gate with a sign that said "Private: Beware of the Goat".

I do not know why the goat concerned me more than the sign did, but I stopped the car. The goat looked at me. I looked at the goat. It was an extraordinarily judgemental animal, and I felt, with the strange clarity of a man who is lost, that it, too, had a view on my navigation.

"You have arrived," said the satnav, with what I thought was needless cruelty.

I reversed down the lane at roughly the speed of a retiring snail, ignoring the voice that kept saying, "When possible, make a U-turn." My passenger, my cousin Gerald, who had spent the journey studying a paper map with the air of a man who distrusts all technology, said it would have been quicker to ask the goat. Gerald is a man of strong opinions and an unfortunate lack of useful ones.

By the time we reached the church, the bride had already walked up the aisle, and I slid into the back pew in the manner of a criminal attending his own trial. A woman beside me whispered that I had missed the vows. I whispered that I had been delayed by a goat. She nodded as though this were an entirely reasonable excuse, which I found oddly comforting.

At the reception, I confessed the whole story to the groom. He laughed so hard that he knocked over a vase. "Lovely village, isn't it?" he said. "Famous for its goats."

On the way home, the satnav was unusually quiet. Somewhere around the second motorway junction, she cleared her throat, if a machine can do that, and said, "In four hundred yards, you have my sincere apologies." I do not believe she said it. But I think of it often.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Не касайтесь нёба кончиком языка, оттяните его назад и слегка округлите губы.
Кончик языка между зубами и звонкий голос. Не заменяйте на з.
Краткий задний звук с округлёнными губами, похож на русское о, но короче и более открытый.
Соединяйте слова: «э-сорт-ов», «слид-инту»: согласный в конце переходит в гласный следующего слова.

questions.question: What began the argument with the satnav?
questions.answer: A misunderstanding about a roundabout exit.

questions.question: What was at the end of the track?
questions.answer: A gate with a sign warning about a goat.

questions.question: Who sat beside the narrator in the car?
What was the village famous for?
